name: Andrew Carnegie
summary: Andrew Carnegie, the steel magnate, defended competition, private property and trusts and tariff protection for American steel, argued in the Gospel of Wealth that the rich owe their surplus to the community and should be heavily taxed at death, opposed American imperialism and campaigned for international arbitration, while his firm broke the Homestead union in 1892.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: In Triumphant Democracy he attacked the 'monstrous system' of the House of Lords, Church and State, primogeniture and entail and an 'arrogant class of drones', praising a republic that gives every citizen equal rights and privileges.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: In 1910 he gave $10 million to found the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, charging its trustees in the deed of gift to hasten the abolition of international war, and Carnegie wanted America to lead in settling disputes among nations by international arbitration.

ban-cartels.rationale: In 1900 he argued that trusts cannot thwart the laws of competition and so prove beneficial agencies for the people, and criticised the popular outcry against them; in The Empire of Business he separated trusts that increase production and reduce prices from harmful ones.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: He argued that surplus wealth is best administered by the individual man of wealth for those who help themselves, and called an able beggar more dangerous to society than a score of wordy Socialists.

class-collaboration.rationale: In 'An Employer's View of the Labor Question' he held that arbitration is the most beneficial remedy, that there is no excuse for a strike or lockout until arbitration has been offered and refused, and that the workers' right to combine will sooner or later be conceded.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: He quoted Disraeli that colonies are millstones round the neck of the mother country and argued dependencies bring a republic burdens, not gain.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: In A League of Peace he proposed that three or more powers form a League that would refer disputes to the Hague or an arbitral body, declare non-intercourse with any nation refusing, and reserve the right to use the necessary force to maintain peace, each member providing forces or money.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: In 'Wealth' he wrote that the law of competition, though hard on the individual, is best for the race because it ensures the survival of the fittest, and that individualism, private property and competition give a better condition than any other system tried.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: In Triumphant Democracy he wrote 'A royal family is an insult to every other family in the land' and wished for the day 'when Royal families are as extinct as dodos', and said he would strike boldly at the royal family as the root of the upas tree.

national-self-determination.rationale: He wrote that the American conscience would not tolerate a war of conquest against the Filipinos and urged the same pledge of independence given to Cuba be given to the Philippines.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: He held that the duty of the man of wealth is to live modestly and administer all surplus revenues as a trust for the community, and his firm's gifts included libraries and a $4 million pension fund for workers.

property-fundamental.rationale: He wrote that the Socialist or Anarchist who seeks to overturn present conditions is attacking the foundation upon which civilization itself rests, which began when the capable workman told the lazy one 'If thou dost not sow, thou shalt not reap'.

separate-church-state.rationale: In Triumphant Democracy he listed Church and State with the House of Lords and primogeniture as branches of the monstrous system he wished to see struck down, and praised the Republic's free public schools.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: In his autobiography he wrote that 'protection has played a great part in the development of manufacturing in the United States' and that the 28 percent duty on steel rails gave his steel business its start.

tax-inheritance.rationale: In 'Wealth' he welcomed the growing disposition to tax more heavily the large estates left at death, noted Pennsylvania's tenth and Britain's graduated death duties, and called a graduated tax on estates the wisest of all taxes.

territorial-expansion.rationale: In 'Distant Possessions' and 'Americanism versus Imperialism' he opposed annexing the Philippines and other distant lands as dependencies that can never be integral parts of the Republic, preferring internal growth.

unions-good.rationale: In the 1892 Homestead dispute the Carnegie Steel firm under Frick cut the rate, shortened contracts, kept the works going with non-union workers protected by 300 Pinkertons and refused to deal with the union, despite his later writings accepting unions.

notes: First audit. Words rest on his 1900 collection of essays and his autobiography; acts rest on Alderson's 1902 biography (the Homestead lockout carried out by his firm under Frick while he was in Scotland, and his libraries and pension fund). Acts and words are kept in separate answers; the unions-good answer follows the lockout against his writings that the right to combine 'must sooner or later be conceded'. Triumphant Democracy, The Empire of Business and A League of Peace were read by theme (monarchy, aristocracy, church, schools, trusts, arbitration, league of nations) and cited for those answers. Searched without a settled answer: Social Darwinism and Spencer (he cites survival of the fittest approvingly in 'Wealth' but states no matching position), religion, women, and free trade (he defends the tariff only as a start for American steel). Most statements are modern and stay null.
